Tuscany
TUS-kuh-nee
n. (the central Italian region of Florence, Siena, Pisa and Lucca, where the evangelical movement of the fifteen-forties took its deepest Italian root and was broken by the Roman Inquisition)
From Latin Tuscia, the land of the Tusci or Etruscans, the people who held the country before Rome.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Tuscany is the region of central Italy between the Apennines and the Tyrrhenian sea, and for the Reformation it is the most important ground in the peninsula that Rome kept. Its cities had printing, banking, universities and a literate laity, and in the fifteen-thirties and forties the writings of Luther, Melanchthon and Bucer travelled its roads in the packs of merchants. Lucca, Siena and Florence all had circles that read justification by faith and said so; Peter Martyr Vermigli preached at Lucca as prior of San Frediano and carried half his convent out of Italy with him in 1542. In that same year Paul the Third reorganised the Roman Inquisition, and the Tuscan movement had perhaps fifteen years before it was hunted down, recanted or scattered to Geneva, Zurich, Strasbourg and the Grisons. Cosimo the First, made duke in 1537 and grand duke in 1569, cooperated with Rome in return for a crown. The dictionary records Tuscany as the clearest case in Europe of a gospel movement that was not defeated by argument but by a tribunal and a prince, and it declines to call that an argument. What survived went abroad and became the Italian exile churches, so that the word which could not be preached in Florence was preached in London and Geneva by Florentines.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a region as a tract of land of indefinite extent; an exile as one banished from his country; a tribunal as a court of justice; a merchant as one who traffics in goods; and a scatter as a dispersion abroad.

expand to see more

REGION, n. A tract of land or space of indefinite extent, usually a tract of some considerable extent; a country; a district.

EXILE, n. Banishment; the state of being expelled from one's native country; also, the person banished.

TRIBUNAL, n. The seat of a judge; a court of justice; the bench on which judges sit.

MERCHANT, n. A man who trafficks or carries on trade with foreign countries, or who exports and imports goods.

SCATTER, v.t. To disperse; to dissipate; to separate and drive in different directions.

Key Scripture

Act 8:4 — "Therefore they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word."

Heb 13:14 — "For here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come."

Act 14:22 — "Confirming the souls of the disciples, and exhorting them to continue in the faith, and that we must through much tribulation enter into the kingdom of God."

Isa 55:11 — "So shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it."

Modern Corruption

Central Italian region whose evangelical circles at Lucca, Siena and Florence were broken by the reorganised Roman Inquisition after 1542, scattering their preachers into the exile churches.

expand to see more

The corruption to name is the modern habit of reading the failure of the Italian Reformation as a verdict on its doctrine, as though a movement that did not win must have been thin. Tuscany refutes that reading. The men who left were not cranks on the edge of the church: they were priors, canons, physicians and professors, and three of them (Vermigli, Ochino, Zanchi) went straight into chairs of divinity in the Reformed cities. What ended the movement was a tribunal with prisons, a prince who wanted a title, and a frontier guarded against books. Luke describes a scattering of exactly this kind and refuses to read it as defeat: “Therefore they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word” (Act 8:4).

The second paragraph names the principle to recover. A gospel movement is not measured by whether it holds a city but by whether the word it carried kept working, and the promise attached to the word does not depend on the magistrate: “it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please” (Isa 55:11). The Tuscan exiles taught their own children that the city they had lost was never the city they were promised, which is the sober word Hebrews gives every displaced believer: “For here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come” (Heb 13:14). Paul had already told the churches what to expect of such years, “that we must through much tribulation enter into the kingdom of God” (Act 14:22).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek diaspeiro (G1289), to scatter abroad; Hebrew dabar (H1697), word; Greek thlipsis (G2347), tribulation.

expand to see more

Greek diaspeiro (G1289) — to scatter abroad, to sow in every direction; “they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word”, Acts 8:4.

Greek kerusso (G2784) — to herald, to proclaim as a crier; “went every where preaching the word”, Acts 8:4.

Hebrew dabar (H1697) — a word, a matter, a thing spoken; “So shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth”, Isaiah 55:11.

Greek thlipsis (G2347) — pressure, affliction, tribulation; “we must through much tribulation enter into the kingdom of God”, Acts 14:22.

Greek polis (G4172) — a city, a walled town; “here have we no continuing city”, Hebrews 13:14.

Usage

"“they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word” (Act 8:4) — what the Tuscan exiles did with their banishment."

"“it shall not return unto me void” (Isa 55:11) — why a broken movement is not a refuted one."

"“For here have we no continuing city” (Heb 13:14) — the lesson the exiles taught their children."
